mcqs.question: Two unrelated processes both load a variable from logical address 0x400000 at the same moment. What does this tell you?
options: One of the two processes must be paused while the other runs
The two processes must be sharing the same physical page
The OS has a bug — no two processes should ever report the same address
This is normal: each process has its own logical address space, and the two logical addresses will be translated to different physical addresses
mcqs.explanation: Logical addresses are per-process; the MMU translates each process's 0x400000 through that process's own translation state, landing on different physical memory. Nothing about this requires pausing, indicates a bug, or implies sharing — it's the entire point of address spaces.

mcqs.question: A process needs to be moved to a different region of physical memory while it keeps running. Which binding time makes this possible?
options: Compile-time binding
Load-time binding
Any binding time, as long as the OS has permission
Execution-time binding
mcqs.explanation: Only execution-time binding defers the logical-to-physical mapping to every individual access, via hardware, so the mapping can change while the process runs. Compile-time and load-time binding both fix the address before or at start, so the process can't be moved afterward without a fault.

mcqs.question: With base = 0x2000 and limit = 0x1000, why does the hardware reject a logical address of 0x1200?
options: 0x1200 is negative when interpreted as a signed offset
0x1200 is a reserved address that no process may ever use
The base register value is invalid
0x1200 is greater than or equal to the limit (0x1000), so it's outside this process's allowed range
mcqs.explanation: The bounds check compares the logical address directly against the limit register; 0x1200 >= 0x1000 fails that check and traps, regardless of the base value. There's no reserved-address rule here and the number isn't negative.

mcqs.question: Given base = 0x14000 and limit = 0x3000, what physical address does logical address 0x2A00 translate to?
options: The access traps — 0x2A00 exceeds the limit
mcqs.explanation: 0x2A00 < limit (0x3000), so the access is allowed; physical = base + logical = 0x14000 + 0x2A00 = 0x16A00. It doesn't trap, and the physical address is neither the bare base nor the bare logical address.

mcqs.question: Why does ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization) depend on execution-time address binding?
options: It doesn't — ASLR works the same way regardless of binding time
ASLR only randomizes physical addresses, which has nothing to do with binding time
Execution-time binding lets the OS place a process's memory regions at a fresh, randomized base each run without recompiling or re-linking the program
ASLR requires compile-time binding so the randomized address can be baked into the binary
mcqs.explanation: ASLR relies on the OS being free to choose (and randomize) load addresses at run time without touching the binary — exactly what execution-time binding provides. Compile-time binding bakes in a fixed address, which is the opposite of what ASLR needs.
